hints: Look closely at what the eyepiece graticule actually is, a little ruler inside the eyepiece with arbitrary units, not micrometres.
Remember which piece of equipment has the known true scale: the stage micrometer is fixed at $10 \mu m$ per small division, so ask yourself which calibrates which.
walkthrough:
**What does an eyepiece graticule do?**

Think of it as a transparent ruler sitting in the eyepiece. It lets you count how many eyepiece units an object covers.

It has no real units by itself, so its value changes with each objective lens.

**Can it compare two cells at x40?**

Yes, lovely and simple. If both cells are viewed with the same x40 objective, the eyepiece units are the same for both.

A cell covering 20 units is bigger than one covering 10 units, even if you do not yet know the value in $\mu m$. No calibration is needed for a relative comparison.

**Can it calibrate a stage micrometer at x10?**

No, this is backwards. The stage micrometer is the standard with a known true length.

You always use the stage micrometer to calibrate the eyepiece graticule, never the eyepiece graticule to calibrate the stage micrometer. So column 1 is possible, column 2 is not possible, which is row B.

options.A: First tick is right, you can compare cells, but second tick is wrong because you cannot calibrate the standard stage micrometer with the eyepiece graticule.
options.B: Exactly right. Comparing relative size is possible with the same objective, but calibrating a stage micrometer is not possible as calibration works the other way round.
options.C: Both parts are reversed. Comparing cells is possible, so the cross is wrong, and calibrating a stage micrometer is not possible, so the tick is wrong.
options.D: Second cross is right, but first cross is wrong because relative comparison of two cells with the same x40 lens is a classic valid use.
